Shmuel entered his zeide’s study with shy, halting steps and a small parcel under his arm. He was a sturdy nineteen-year-old who had inherited the Maharal’s high forehead and deep set eyes, and was in Prague preparing his upcoming wedding. Since childhood, Shmuel had longed to live up to his family name. How he wished he could stay for hours in the beis midrash, master whole masechtos of Shas, and even compose chiddushim of his own. But he simply didn’t have the head for all of that. Perhaps the gift he had brought with him would give his grandfather a different sort of nachas, at least.

“Over the past few years, I’ve been … working on something.” Shmuel

set the package down on the table and unwrapped its paper. Inside was a rectangular box, small enough to fit in his cupped hands, made of white marble and stone. “It’s an aron kodesh. A gift for Zeide.” Shmuel turned the aron around, showing his grandfather its intricate carvings

and squinted as he examined each side. “Beautiful work, Shmelke! This is an image of churban Beis Hamikdash, I see. And here is Chana of the times of the Chashmona’im, holding the hand of her last son. Over here, a wandering Yid, holding a travel stick and a sefer Torah.”

Shmuel lifted the slab of marble from the top of the tiny aron. Inside, there was yet a smaller box carved of black wood. This wooden aron featured a whole new set of engravings, all themed around the Beis Hamikdash. The right side was imprinted with an image of the Beis Hamikdash

LAST TIME: The Maharal and Rav Betzalel return from Worms, greatly impressed with Reb Eliyahu Baal Shem’s love and care for his fellow Jews, as well as his scholarship. They resolve to fight to defend his reputation against those proposing a cherem against him. A New Kind

The original Pinsk yeshiva was supported by an orphan from Karlin named Tevel. Tevel was a humble, kind, but unlearned Jew who hid the wealth which he’d gained from growing his father’s beekeeping business. Tevel regularly gave large sums of money to the Rav of Pinsk to distribute anonymously.

Early one morning, as young Tevel hurried to the shul in Karlin for shacharis, he heard muffled sounds coming from a garden nearby. He listened more closely, and realized that it was a young girl crying. He felt both pity for the poor girl’s suffering, and also curiosity. The Jewish owners of the inn, as far as he knew, led a coarse lifestyle similar to their customers, the local peasants.

Tevel discovered that the young woman was the inn’s newly-hired maid. An orphan from a young age, Chava Devorah had no one to look after her. She had to put up with harsh working conditions and much verbal abuse at the hands of the innkeeper and his wife. With the help of his mentor, the Rav of Pinsk, Tevel rescued Chava Devorah from the inn. He eventually married her, and gave her half of his fortune to use as she pleased.

Chava Devorah had taught herself to read and understand the basic Hebrew of Chumash, which made her the more learned of the two. She began to teach Tevel what she knew. As the young couple advanced in their studies, they hired a young Torah scholar to live with them and teach them more Torah. Over time, they both became quite knowledgeable. But, like the money that they gave to tzedakah, they kept their learning a secret.

Meanwhile, the old Rav of Pinsk left and was replaced by Rav Naftali Katz of Prague (who we will meet in the following chapter). Rav Naftali soon insisted that Tevel and Chava Devorah reveal their generosity to the public, so that all of Pinsk may learn from and model their kindness. They agreed to do so, but only if they could avoid any resulting honor by moving far away. Thus, after forty years of supporting the Pinsk yeshiva in secret, the middle-aged couple moved on to Cracow—but not before the local yeshiva received a new name due to their generous support: Tevel and Chava Devorah’s Yeshiva.

There were three distinguished yeshivos in Pinsk. The first and oldest one was “Tevel and Chava Devorah’s Yeshiva”, another was called “Reb Shimon’s Yeshiva”, and the one most recently built was known as “Bubbe Golda Leah’s Yeshiva”. Each of those men and women were Baalei tzedakah who supported the yeshivos, and each had a fascinating story behind their donation.

The second famous Pinsk yeshiva was called Reb Shimon’s Yeshiva. Reb Shimon was a nephew of the Maharshal, Reb Shlomo Luria. Reb Shimon did not have the head for learning, but he loved Torah with all his heart. So, when Reb Shimon went into the diamond business, he was determined to use his wealth to support yeshivos. His first project was in his hometown of Pinsk: he convinced a learned relative to come to Pinsk to found a new yeshiva, and promised to fund it.

But he didn’t stop there. During his many business travels, Reb Shimon observed how the poor kehillos of Poland and Lithuania lacked structured schools of learning. And so, he dedicated his efforts to helping these communities establish yeshivos, too.

Once, on his birthday, he and his wife discovered a buried treasure of many clay pitchers brimming with gold coins. He drew up a contract with the Rav, whereby they committed most of the buried treasure to support hundreds of yeshivos throughout Eastern Europe.

“Bubbe” Golda Leah was a midwife by profession, who was at the side of every woman in town who gave birth. But this extraordinary lady was involved in helping the Pinsk community in many other ways, too. Most of all, she dedicated herself for the sick, visiting their homes to care for them and their families personally. She often pulled her husband away from his work as a tailor to help in these vital efforts.

She was also a mikvah attendant and Torah teacher. She taught the local women how to completely live their lives according to the Torah, influencing them to refine their middos and inspiring them with stories of righteous women through the ages.

Bubbe Golda Leah was also known to give brachos to women who were suffering from miscarriage, stillborns, or sickly children. News of her success spread throughout the region, far beyond Pinsk. She refused payment for her services, but when a woman insisted, she would pass the funds on for a newly- established yeshiva. While the other two yeshivos in Pinsk were mainly for married men, this yeshiva was unique in that it was for younger bachurim.

Bubbe Golda Leah soon became the yeshiva’s main donor. Over time, as her fame increased, her contributions grew, and the yeshiva became known as “Bubbe Golda Leah’s Yeshiva”.
